title: India's Got Latent Is Back, and Netflix Is Daring You to Watch It Without a Filter
excerpt: Sixteen months after a single sentence detonated his career, Samay Raina returns tonight at 7 PM IST — simulcast on Netflix and YouTube, with the comment section deliberately torn out.
body:
The promo opens like a setup to a joke that already knows it's dangerous. **Samay Raina** is mid-banter with longtime collaborator **Balraj Singh Ghai**, swatting away the obvious question — why would anyone pay for Netflix when the show is free on YouTube? Then a man pretending to be a Netflix employee leans in with the kicker: there's no comment section on Netflix, so the trolls can't reach you. Samay doesn't flinch. *"Gaaliyaan toh padenge aur woh hum denge, kyunke hamare show mein koi filter bhi nahi hota,"* he shoots back, before pressing a nimbu-mirchi into the man's hand like a blessing and a warning at once.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=yzW3qv7reOg</youtube>

https://x.com/NetflixIndia/status/2068328872060317993

That one line tells you everything about where this comeback sits. **India's Got Latent Season 2** premieres tonight, June 20, at 7 PM IST — and in a first-of-its-kind move for an Indian production, it streams on Netflix and YouTube *simultaneously*. New episodes drop every two weeks. The only difference between the two platforms, Samay deadpans, is that Netflix viewers won't be interrupted by ads, and they won't get a comment box to scream into. Given how Season 1 ended, that second detail is less a feature than a fortification.


> "Gaaliyaan toh padenge aur woh hum denge, kyunke hamare show mein koi filter bhi nahi hota." — Samay Raina

Let's not pretend the elephant isn't in the room. The first season of *India's Got Latent* didn't quietly wind down — it was blown apart. In early 2025, a remark by guest **Ranveer Allahbadia** during an episode triggered a national firestorm: multiple FIRs, legal challenges, Supreme Court intervention, and a comedy ecosystem suddenly relitigating where the line sits. The show vanished from YouTube. For a long, ugly stretch, it looked like the most-watched comedy experiment in the Indian creator economy had been legislated out of existence.

What makes this return feel earned rather than opportunistic is how Samay played the silence. In April 2026, on a stand-up stage in front of a crowd that had lived every beat of the saga with him, he landed what may be his sharpest line yet: *"I don't think Season 1 of my show could have ended in a better way."* The room understood. It wasn't defiance for its own sake — it was a comedian metabolising the worst year of his professional life into material, then walking back toward the fire on his own terms.

Now Netflix is holding the matches. The platform announced a double-barrelled collaboration: the return of *India's Got Latent* and an all-new Samay Raina stand-up special currently in development, exclusive to Netflix, with no title or date yet. The teaser even brought back **Amin Khan**, the bodyguard who became a fan favourite during Samay's *Still Alive* special — a wink to the diehards who never left.

There is, of course, a louder conversation humming underneath all this. Netflix is dropping *India's Got Latent* and the equally provocative *Lock Upp 2* within a week of each other, and critics are already asking whether controversy has quietly become the platform's growth strategy in a brutally competitive Indian OTT market. The cynical read writes itself: take the show that got too hot for YouTube and hand it a global megaphone. The generous read is that a genuinely original format — raw, improvised, gleefully unpolished — deserved a second act, and a deep-pocketed backer was always going to be the way it got one.

For the diaspora, the simulcast is the real headline. NRIs in the US, UK, and Canada who spent Season 1 hunting for reuploads and dodging geo-blocks can now watch in real time, ad-free, the moment it drops — the same 7 PM IST premiere, the same chaos, just minus the buffering and the bile. The YouTube version stays free and global; the Netflix version is the polished, padded room.

Whether Season 2 can recapture the unhinged magic of the original without the comment-section colosseum egging it on is the open question. Comedy this combustible often draws its energy from the danger of going too far. Samay seems to know exactly what he's walking back into — and this time, he's the one holding the nimbu mirchi.
